p.title: Strategic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying
p.venue: MIT Political Science Department Research Paper 2021-2 (later listed as The Journal of Politics 88(1), 2026, per Paul's docx)

ext.title: Strategic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying
authors: Jan Stuckatz (Institute for Advanced Study in Toulouse)
ext.venue: MIT Political Science Department Research Paper No. 2021-2; SSRN 3937466. Dated October 15, 2020 in the text. The Journal of Politics 88(1), 2026 listing from the metadata hint does not appear anywhere in the PDF text, so it is unverified here.
ext.document_type: Working paper ("Do Not Cite or Circulate Without Permission from Author")
ext.coverage: Full text read: all 250k characters of _text/331171275468.txt. Main text (pp. 1-24), references (pp. 25-28), and Appendices A-F (pp. 1-7 of the appendix) were read in full. Roughly 1,100 lines of the file are a column of lone "G" characters from a figure's node layout and were skipped as non-text; the figure labels around them were read. Paul's markup: all 64 entries in _annots/331171275468.json were read (the only annotation file for this work). Every entry is a Highlight with empty note content. The copyright rule limits quoting, so covered text is paraphrased rather than reproduced; page numbers are PDF page indices (printed page = PDF page - 2). Note: the metadata hint says 1999-2018 data and an SSRN date; the text shows the dating used below.
ext.research_question: Are campaign donations and lobbying activity linked for the same interest group-politician pair, and do donations precede lobbying on bills tied to the donee's committee seats, sponsorship or co-sponsorship (the "access-buying" hypothesis)?
ext.theory: Two camps on campaign money: donations as ideology or electoral competition (Poole and Romer 1985; Poole, Romer and Rosenthal 1987) versus donations as long-term strategic investments for access (Langbein 1986; Austen-Smith 1995; Esterling 2007; Richter and Werner 2017; Barber, Canes-Wrone and Thrower 2017). Lobbying either conveys information (Austen-Smith and Wright 1992; Potters and Van Winden 1992) or serves as a legislative subsidy to allies (Hall and Deardorff 2006). The paper tests the access-buying direction (donation precedes lobbying) and sets aside rewards (fn 9).
ext.data: Unit: firm-politician-year dyad. Sample: all publicly traded U.S. manufacturing firms (NAICS 31-33; 2,703 firms that lobbied or donated at least once) and all 979 members of the House and Senate serving 2008-2018 (text uses 2008-2017 in places). Result: an unbalanced panel of 2,646,237 unique firm-politician dyads and 16,428,834 observations. Sources: Lobbying Disclosure Act reports (over 1.2 million parsed; over 75 million reports plus FEC filings combined since 1999 per abstract; lobbying data from 1999, bill-level quality from 2008 after the HLOGA amendment); FEC itemized contributions (about 53 million individual contributions, four million employer names, 827,000 occupation names, 1980-2018); Compustat gvkey; SOC codes; GovTrack IDs; Volden and Wiseman (2018) politician covariates; Groseclose and Stewart (1998) committee scores. Broader descriptive coverage: over 84,000 interest groups (abstract, p. 2). Descriptive 2013 snapshot: 11,829 public companies and 553 members of Congress (6,541,437 possible dyads). Appendix E: 1999/2000 interest-group comparison.
ext.method: Step 1: descriptive tables and cross-sectional log-log fits (Table 2, Fig 2, Appendix C and E). Step 2: linear probability models with firm, year, politician and firm-politician fixed effects, with controls for party, majority status, committee chair and powerful-committee membership (Table 3, Table F.1; standard errors clustered by firm). Step 3: difference-in-differences combined with matching (Imai, Kim and Wang 2020). Treated pairs are first-time donors defined over L = 3 years. Matched controls are other firms with no donation to the same politician in t to t-3. Matching uses Mahalanobis distance on sales, employees and pre-treatment lobbying, with 10 closest comparators. The DiD estimator (Eq. 4) differences outcome changes between t-1 and t+F for treated pairs versus the matched mean, averaged over pairs. Confidence intervals come from a block bootstrap. Outcome: Y=1 if the firm lobbies a bill that is sponsored, co-sponsored, or assigned to a committee on which the politician serves (each measured separately).
ext.scope: Population: publicly traded U.S. manufacturing firms and House and Senate members, 2008-2017/2018 (main analysis). Institution: U.S. Congress and federal lobbying disclosure. Era: LDA electronic filing era (1999 on; bill-level data from 2008). Excludes private firms, trade and industry associations, ideological groups, unions and nonprofits from the main analysis. Congress is the relevant lobbied institution; agencies are about 3.4% of reports (p. 5).

key_findings.finding: Descriptive 2013 snapshot: only 519 of 11,829 public companies (about 4%) both donated and lobbied, yet they account for most money in politics.
Firm-politician dyads with both donations and bill-related lobbying are extremely rare but carry large money: 13,886 dyads out of 6,541,437 possible.
key_findings.location: Sec 2.1, printed p. 13 (PDF p. 15), Table 2 right panel
key_findings.numbers: 13,886 dyads (<0.1% of all possible); more than $520 million, 17% of 2013 spending; 15,420 donation-only dyads, 13,078 of them from employee donations

key_findings.finding: Firm-level corporate PAC donations and lobbying spending are positively related for firms doing both.
key_findings.numbers: Log-log slope beta = 0.88, adjusted R2 about 0.4; text says a 10% PAC increase goes with 8.8% more lobbying, while the Fig 2 caption computes 8.7%

key_findings.finding: Other donation types show the same firm-level pattern (all donations, executives, employees, government relations).
key_findings.numbers: beta 0.58 (R2 0.29) all donations; 0.58 (0.17) executives; 0.68 (0.23) employees; 0.78 (0.20) government relations; years 2000-2017

key_findings.finding: Within firm-politician pairs, a firm's first-time donation raises the probability it lobbies a bill tied to that politician in the same year.
key_findings.numbers: Donation coefficient 0.102-0.118 (SEs about 0.008-0.009), N = 16,428,834. Firm-politician and year FE (last column) gives 0.118. Baseline probability about 0.05; sponsors 0.002, co-sponsors 0.026, committee members 0.043

key_findings.finding: Donation amount matters at the margin: a 10% larger first-time donation goes with about 0.15 percentage points higher probability of lobbying a related bill.
key_findings.numbers: Donation Amount coefficient 0.015-0.017 per log unit (SE 0.001); about 0.15 pp per 10%

key_findings.finding: Under difference-in-differences with matching, a donation raises the probability the pair lobbies related bills by about 8.5 points in the donation year, falling to about 3 points by three years later.
key_findings.location: Sec 3.2, Fig 5 (printed p. 20-21); caption gives 8.5 falling to 3.2 pp
key_findings.numbers: Senate t+0 about 0.085, t+3 about 0.03; House effects larger (no number given in text); effects disappear within two to three years

key_findings.finding: Effects are concentrated in committee-related lobbying. Corporate PAC donations show the largest effects, but CEO and employee donations are also positive. The same-firm sponsor link is positive but short-lived.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative: committee effects largest; PAC > CEO and employee; no numeric values in text

key_findings.finding: Robustness to firm-level covariates (sales, employees) leaves the donation coefficient essentially unchanged.
key_findings.numbers: Donation coefficient 0.104-0.123 across eight models; N = 7,189,477 for covariate-controlled models; adjusted R2 0.450-0.544

key_findings.finding: The Ansolabehere, Snyder and Tripathi (2002) pattern holds for the 1999/2000 interest-group data, with the strongest PAC-lobbying relation for corporations.
key_findings.location: Appendix E, Fig E.1 (appendix p. 6); cube-root scale
key_findings.numbers: beta: corporations 2.0; membership organizations 1.6; trade associations 0.8; labor unions 0.6 (described as not present)

key_findings.finding: Illustrative cases: Farenthold (Exxon Mobil PAC) and Lockheed Martin-Bill Nelson show donations followed by related bills and sponsorship.
key_findings.numbers: Farenthold received $3,000 from Exxon's PAC in his first year; Nelson received $9,000 from Lockheed's PAC in 2011 and $22,000 from executives and employees in 2012

limitations: Main analysis covers only publicly traded U.S. manufacturing firms; private firms, trade associations, ideological groups and unions are excluded (printed p. 24).
Donations through industry associations, ideological groups and nonprofits are not captured; the authors say this may understate donation effects on access (printed p. 24).

Lobbying-to-politician links rely on bills named in LDA reports. Per-bill lobbying dollars are allocated evenly across connected politicians, which the authors call a highly noisy measure (printed p. 8). Bill success is not modeled (printed p. 24).
Access-buying is inferred from timing, not from measured private connections; the reverse (rewards) direction is explicitly left for future work (fn 9, printed p. 14-15).
Name disambiguation is heuristic with hand validation; a graph neural network upgrade is noted as in progress (fn 6, printed p. 6).

Sample period is stated inconsistently: abstract and Sec 2 say 2000 or 1999 onward, p. 2 says 2000-2018, p. 12 says 2008-2018, and the main estimates use 2008-2017. Donation-to-lobbying elasticity is 8.8% in text versus 8.7% in the Fig 2 caption. Fig C.1 caption says cubed USD while the axes are logged.

Effects are estimated relative to a low base rate (about 0.05), so 8.5 points is large in relative terms but small in levels. The linear probability models rely on parametric assumptions, as the paper acknowledges (printed p. 17). The DiD estimator is conservative and underpowered per Imai, Kim and Wang (2020), per fn 18.
Estimates are associations within matched designs, not proof of quid pro quo; the paper itself disclaims causal reading of the reverse direction.
Journal publication is not in the PDF; the 2026 Journal of Politics listing is taken from the metadata hint only.

measures: Donation indicator: first-time donation by firm i to politician j in year t, with a 3-year no-donation window (L = 3).
Outcome Y: 1 if firm lobbies a bill tied to politician j via sponsorship, co-sponsorship, or committee assignment.
Lobby $: firm lobbying per year divided by bills lobbied, allocated across connected politicians (described as noisy).
PAC $, CEO $, employee donations (disaggregated by donor type; government relations and executive categories in Appendix C).
Firm sales and employees (Compustat); pre-treatment lobbying (matching covariates).

Politician covariates: party, majority status, committee chair, powerful-committee membership (top four Groseclose-Stewart committees: Appropriations, Armed Services, Finance, Rules and Administration).
Interest-group type classes (corporations, trade associations, labor unions, ideological and membership groups) from NAICS codes (Appendix E).
references_of_note: Ansolabehere, Snyder and Tripathi 2002, Business and Politics 4(2): direct precursor linking PAC donations and lobbying, 1997-98 House data; the paper replicates it with 1999/2000 data (Appendix E).

Kim and Kunisky 2020, Political Analysis (forthcoming), 'Mapping Political Communities: A Statistical Analysis of Lobbying Networks in Legislative Politics': the lobbying-network data the paper builds on; the most direct network reference.
Imai, Kim and Wang 2020, 'Matching Methods for Causal Inference with Time-Series Cross-Section Data' (working paper): the matched DiD estimator used here.
Kalla and Broockman 2016, AJPS: randomized field experiment on donor access to officials; the paper's closest experimental precedent.
Powell and Grimmer 2016, JOP 'Money in Exile': PACs seek short-term access to committees; matches the transient effect found here.
Fouirnaies and Hall 2018, AJPS; Lorenz 2020, JOP: committee-membership and coalition lobbying; relevant to the committee-related effects.
Hall and Deardorff 2006, APSR: lobbying as legislative subsidy; theory contrast.
Fowler, Garro and Spenkuch 2020, JOP 'Quid pro quo? Corporate returns to campaign contributions': the paper cites it as finding no quid-pro-quo returns to PAC donations.
Kang 2015, REStud; Huneeus and Kim 2019: returns to corporate lobbying; cited as the contrast to donation returns.
Bonica 2014 (AJPS, ideology mapping) and Bonica 2017 (DIME): donation data and ideology scores the paper warns may be strategic rather than ideological.
Groseclose and Stewart 1998, AJPS: committee value scores used for the powerful-committee covariate.
Volden and Wiseman 2018, JOP: politician-level legislative effectiveness covariates.
Enamorado, Fifield and Imai 2019, APSR (fastLink): probabilistic record linkage for FEC candidate IDs.
Schaeffer 2007, Computer Science Review: graph clustering used for named-entity disambiguation.
Li 2018, APSR; Richter and Werner 2017, JLEO: PAC constraints and executive donations; relevant to donor-type heterogeneity.
Bertrand et al. 2020, AER: corporate philanthropy as a further channel of political influence.
Wilkerson, Smith and Stramp 2015, AJPS: text reuse for tracing policy ideas across bills; relevant to bill-success limitation.

rel.summary_md:
Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters link LDA bill mentions to FEC donations for U.S. public manufacturing firms (2,703 firms, 979 members of Congress, 2008-2017, 16.4M firm-politician-year rows). They test whether a donation comes before lobbying on bills that the recipient sponsored, cosponsored or handled in committee. In the descriptive 2013 snapshot, only 519 of 11,829 public firms both donated and lobbied, and they account for about 85% of the money. Under firm-politician fixed effects, a first-time donation (no gift in the prior 3 years) goes with a 10-12 point higher chance of lobbying a related bill in the same year, against a base rate of about 0.05. Matched difference-in-differences gives about 8.5 points at year t (Senate), falling to about 3 points by t+3. The effect is concentrated in committee-related lobbying and is largest for corporate PACs. The authors read this as access-buying timing, not quid pro quo.

For Paul's systems, the paper matters mainly because its estimand differs from what the system measured. The FEC-to-LDA bridge (round 3) is a cross-sectional member-by-industry-by-cycle rank correlation. It is dominated by trade associations, credits only sponsors and cosponsors, and controls for finance-committee seats. Its four-control partial of about 0 does not contradict a within-pair, onset-timed, committee-driven effect among public firms. The bridge design actually controls away the channel Kim finds strongest. The paper also cuts against the system's "FEC leads LDA by 42 months" heuristic: its effect is concurrent and gone within two to three years.

The paper also builds its outcome from the same bill-roster join that the system ruled circular. It escapes circularity only because its treatment, the donation, is timed independently of the join. Its identity work (gvkey matching, constrained graph clustering, hand-coded validation) is a method source for Mentat's donor ladder. Every figure here is the paper's own; none has been reproduced locally (UNVERIFIED per DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Within firm-politician pairs, a first-time donation (L=3 no-donation window) raises P(lobby a related bill) by 0.102-0.118 (FE LPM, N=16,428,834, base ~0.05). Matched DiD: about +8.5 pp at t (Senate), about +3 pp at t+3, gone within 2-3 years. Effects are largest for committee-related bills and corporate PACs. Unit: public manufacturing firms, 2008-2017.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 3.1 Table 3 (printed p. 16-17); Sec 3.2 Figs 5-6 (printed p. 20-22)
bearings.system_side: Bridge round 3 is a locked corroboration look. X is FEC relational exposure and Y is rebuilt LDA attention, per member x industry (credit_union, fintech, crypto) x cycle, 2023-2026. It uses pooled fractional-rank Spearman with member-blocked permutation and four controls: party, chamber, volume-within-party, and House Financial Services/Senate Banking membership. Result: raw rho +0.153 (p=.0146) but four-control partial -0.0002, UNCORROBORATED, predictor language barred, window CLOSED. The brain also carries 'FEC leads LDA 42 months' as a candidate heuristic.
bearings.code_ref: fec_lda_bridge3_prereg.md:1-30,95-115; fec/lobbying/fec_lda_bridge3_look.py:30-60 (YEARS, INDUSTRIES, CONTROL_NAMES incl. committee); brain actors/lobbyview-collector.md:124,137
bearings.transfer_conditions: The two estimands differ. Kim identifies within-pair timing, with pair FE or matched DiD and first-time donation onset. The bridge tests a between-member cross-section with concurrent windows. The bridge's finance-committee control absorbs the very channel Kim finds strongest. Its Y credits only sponsor and cosponsor rosters, with no committee channel. Its clients are mostly trade associations (ABA, CUNA), which Kim excludes; his Appendix E gives a weaker PAC-lobbying slope for trade associations (0.8) than for corporations (2.0). So the bridge null does not refute Kim, and Kim does not license predictor language in the system. Kim's concurrent effect that fades within 2-3 years also contradicts a 42-month lead. A successor test that honors Kim would need onset events, a pair panel and a committee-referral outcome; that is a new prereg and is Paul's gate.

bearings.paper_claim: Outcome Y=1 if the firm lobbies a bill sponsored, cosponsored or committee-assigned to politician j. Per-bill lobbying dollars are spread evenly across connected politicians, which the authors call a highly noisy measure. Donation timing is the independent treatment.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 2 data (printed p. 5-8); Sec 3 outcome definition (printed p. 14-15)
bearings.system_side: The member link is manufactured by crediting every sponsor and cosponsor of a lobbied bill. P(joined | lobbied)=1 by construction, so it is REFUTED as evidence of influence. LD-2 never names members.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Kim uses the same roster join, but only as an outcome against a treatment (donation onset) that is measured outside the join. That is the non-circular use the brain's 'which side of the join' test allows. It supports keeping the join as 'whose bills did this org lobby on' and never as contact. Kim also adds a committee-referral channel that the system's join lacks (only sponsor and cosponsor roles exist). The paper gives no warrant to read the join as a contact measure.

bearings.paper_claim: The donation-to-lobbying link is driven by FIRST-TIME donations (no gift to that member in t-1..t-3). It is concurrent (year t) and decays to about 3 pp by t+3. Corporate PAC > CEO/employee donations, and all are positive. Committee-related bills dominate.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 3.1 design (printed p. 14-15); Sec 3.2 Figs 5-6 (printed p. 20-22)
bearings.system_side: Channel C3, donation co-occurrence, builds org-PAC (and, with G1, lobbyist) money reaching member m near quarter q as gave-in-quarter, gave-in-cycle and amount tiers. Zero is no-evidence, and donation-predicts-lobbying wording is barred. Channel C2 is dated committee venue on cited bills.
bearings.transfer_conditions: These are design hints only: an onset feature (first gift to m in 3 years) instead of gave-in-cycle, a short decay horizon, and a C2 x C3 interaction (committee venue). They must fit the hard cap of 10 fused features and the prereg/one-look discipline. Kim's outcome is lobbying a related bill, not a contact, so the paper cannot serve as validation (LobbyView-lineage bar). Sample transfer is weak: public manufacturing firms versus financial associations and CUs.

bearings.paper_claim: Donation-linked lobbying effects are concentrated in committee-related bills rather than sponsorship, and firms target politicians with legislative power over their industry (committee jurisdiction).
bearings.system_side: Influence% = committee_raw/MAX, from CU-relevance-tiered seats (Highly 3.0 / Moderately 1.8 / Slightly 0.9; subcommittee 1/6) plus a leadership multiplier. It is weighted 40% in the composite.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The qualitative point carries over: interest-group money and lobbying converge on members who hold jurisdiction, which supports treating CU-relevant seats as structural leverage. The paper says nothing about the tier weights, the subcommittee 1/6 factor or the chair ladder. Its 'powerful committee' covariate is Groseclose-Stewart (Appropriations, Armed Services, Finance, Rules), not Financial Services or Banking. The sample is manufacturing firms.

bearings.paper_claim: FEC has no unique donor IDs (about 53M contributions, 4M employer strings, 827k occupations). The authors standardize names (Bonica 2017), match employers to Compustat gvkey and occupations to SOC codes (executives = SOC 11-1011), and run unsupervised constrained graph clustering on address, donation history and targets. They cross-validate against hand-coded ground truth and revise corporate PACs manually.
bearings.system_side: A rule-based ladder (AUTO / HIGH / REVIEW / DISCARD). Exact name + same zip gives AUTO; exact name + same zip across employers gives HIGH; anything below threshold is DISCARD. There is no name-frequency weighting. Employer assignment uses a strict-names roster.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The method transfers directly, since both work on the same FEC Schedule A data. The paper reports no precision or recall, so it is a design reference, not a benchmark. Adopting graph clustering would loosen Mentat's strict-names rule, and receipt-counting is frozen without a per-change OK. Any change is Paul's call. The paper's hand-coded validation step is the transferable piece: a labelled sample to measure the ladder's precision and recall.

bearings.paper_claim: Donations buy access in timing terms: lobbying follows donations at year t and decays within 2-3 years. The paper measures lobbying activity, not votes, and cites Fowler, Garro and Spenkuch (2020) for no quid-pro-quo returns.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract (printed p. 1); Sec 3.2 (printed p. 20-22); intro (printed p. 2-4)
bearings.system_side: Money is the minority partner (WM 0.35 vs WP 0.65), justified in the code comment as 'money buys access/effort > votes'. CU and industry money enter as static levels (congestion.json cu, banks+finserv) with Michaelis-Menten saturation on receipts. There is no onset or recency term.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper is consistent with the access-not-votes stance but gives no vote-shift evidence, so it cannot calibrate WM/WP or HALFF. It does imply that the access value of money is transient and onset-driven, which a static cycle-level money term ignores. The sample is public manufacturing firms; the system models CU/bank PACs.

gaps_exposed: The bridge's Y (rebuilt LDA attention) credits only sponsor and cosponsor rosters. The committee-referral channel, which carries Kim's largest effect, is absent from the join even though build_network_2021_rebuild.py parses committee_referrals. The committee control then absorbs whatever committee-driven signal is left.

There is no within-pair, onset-timed design anywhere in the system. Every FEC-LDA test is cross-sectional and concurrent, so Kim's estimand (first-time donation, then lobbying in the same year, matched DiD) has never been tested locally.

The system has no measure of how long an access effect lasts. Money enters the flip model and C3 as cycle-level levels; Kim shows the effect fades within 2-3 years and is concentrated at donation onset.

There is no firm-level (corporate) identity layer in the lobbying lane. Clients are mostly associations, which Kim excludes and finds weaker for (trade-association slope 0.8 vs corporations 2.0, Appendix E).
Mentat's identity ladder has no measured precision or recall. Kim's hand-coded cross-validation is the missing step.
flags: D-021: Kim builds firm-politician edges and weights (Fig 1; per-bill lobbying $ allocated across connected politicians) from LDA bill mentions. Adopting that construction would make LDA an edge and weight source. Use LDA only for identity; any edge would have to come from the donation side or another source.

The bridge round 3 standing ruling bars presenting FEC exposure as a lobbying predictor, and a different control set on the 2023-2026 window is NOT a successor. Kim's result must not be pasted into Melange surfaces as 'donations predict lobbying'. It is external evidence on a different population and estimand, UNVERIFIED locally (DE-062).

Pooled figure: the abstract's 8.5 pp is the Senate t+0 DiD point. The House is larger (no number given) and donor types differ (PAC > CEO/employee). Quote it as '+8.5 pp, Senate, first-time donation, year t, public manufacturing firms 2008-2017, base ~0.05'; otherwise label it UNSTRATIFIED.
'Access' in the paper is the authors' interpretation of timing. It must not be carried over as an access or closeness probability for any system output (D-025).

Internal inconsistencies in the source: elasticity 8.8% in the text vs 8.7% in the Fig 2 caption; sample period given variously as 1999, 2000-2018, 2008-2018 and 2008-2017; the Fig C.1 caption says cubed USD while the axes are logged. Paul's annotation cites the work as 'Systemic and sequential links...' (JOP 2026), but this PDF is titled 'Strategic and Sequential Links...' and dated 2020; the JOP listing is unverified from the PDF.
The paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, so neither rejected SNA proposal is implicated.

The '42-month lead' heuristic in the brain (lobbyview-collector.md:124) conflicts with Kim's finding of a concurrent effect that fades within 2-3 years. The heuristic should stay a candidate only and must not cite this paper.
rel.paul_alignment: This partly agrees with Paul's expectation that donations lead lobbying (his fec-lda-bridge position cites this paper). The agreement holds only at the firm-politician dyad, within pair, at donation onset and over a short horizon. The system's bridge null (four-control partial -0.0002) does not make his note wrong, but the note is now underspecified. It needs the estimand distinction: within-pair onset timing versus cross-sectional member-by-industry, corporations versus trade associations, and committee-referral versus sponsor/cosponsor credit. The paper also weakens the '42-month lead' framing that sits beside his note. His highlights of gvkey/SOC matching, constrained graph clustering and hand-coded validation (Mentat employer-match and identity-ladder positions) are accurate, and Mentat's strict-names rule is indeed more conservative. His committee-pillar reading (effects strongest in committee activity) matches the paper. His media-blend note citing a 2-3 year fade is accurate about the paper, but that fade measures donation-to-lobbying access, not stance salience, so it should not set press or social half-lives.

related.why: A later version of the same Kim-Stuckatz-Wolters project (the title Paul cites as JOP 2026). Its estimates should supersede the ones in this 2020 working paper where they differ.
The paper builds on the Kim-Kunisky lobbying-network data and bill-politician linkage for its firm-politician dyads.
The LobbyView firm-bill database is the LDA-side source; it is the same lineage Paul's contact-inference memos treat as a cautionary chain.
Imai and Kim's critique of two-way fixed effects motivates this paper's switch from FE LPMs to matched DiD for time-series cross-section data.
A field experiment showing that donor status raises access to officials; it is the experimental counterpart to Kim's observational timing evidence.

Both find low overlap between lobbying and PAC organizations (Kim: about 4% of public firms do both, yet hold about 85% of the money). Furnas emphasizes the low overlap; Kim emphasizes the dyad link among the overlapping firms.
Cited as evidence on returns to corporate lobbying, in contrast to the absence of donation returns.
The paper uses Bonica's DIME donor data and name standardization, and warns that donation-based ideology scores may reflect strategy rather than ideology.
A review of empirical lobbying models that places this paper's combined donation-and-lobbying linkage design in context.
